title: The Night Before the Exam
tagline: A student reads her notes three times and feels sure. Then she sits the exam. Why feeling you know is not the same as knowing, and how to study so that it lasts.
card: A study plan that puts together roots, verb families, pegs and formula characters, built on testing yourself rather than re-reading.
goal: you will see why re-reading fools us, use a five-step study cycle that combines the tools from this wing, and test yourself on all four kinds of material.

left_off.q: What is the first step in memorising a formula?
left_off.a: Say what it means in words. Meaning comes before pictures.

left_off.q: What character is c in E = mc²?

text: It is eleven at night in a university library, and a student, Lena, has an exam at nine in the morning. She has a stack of notes: forty new words, twenty irregular verbs, a list of ten steps for a procedure, and four formulas. She has three hours before the library closes, and she is calm, because she has a plan. She will read it all again, three times.

She does. She reads the words and each one feels familiar. She reads the verbs and they look right. By one o'clock she has a warm, comfortable feeling that she knows it. She goes to bed pleased with herself.

check.a: She planned to read all her notes again, three times.

parts.talk: How do you usually study the night before an exam? Does it work?

text: At nine o'clock the exam begins, and the first question is a blank page. The words are not there. The verbs she thought she knew will not come out. She stares at a formula and cannot remember how it starts. It is the strangest feeling: everything looks familiar, but nothing comes when she asks for it.

What went wrong? Recognising is not recalling. When she read the notes, every word was in front of her, and the feeling of familiarity was strong. In the exam the notes were gone, and the memory had never been trained to come out on its own.

check.q: What is the difference between recognising and recalling?
check.a: Recognising is seeing something and feeling it is familiar; recalling is bringing it out with nothing in front of you. Only recall has been trained when you test yourself.

parts.talk: Can you remember a time when you felt sure you knew something, but could not produce it? What happened?

text: Psychologists have tested this many times. In one well-known series of experiments, students studied a short text and then either read it again or tried to recall it from memory. A week later, the students who had tested themselves remembered clearly more than those who had simply re-read, even though the re-readers felt more confident.

That is the lesson of this room, and the lesson of the whole library wing. Words, verbs, steps and formulas all need the same treatment: understand, picture, place, test, and come back. You will practise all four kinds at once, as in the exam.

check.q: What did the experiments show about testing yourself?
check.a: Students who tested themselves remembered more after a week than those who only re-read, even though they felt less confident.

parts.talk: What will you change about the way you study after hearing this?

words.m: known; seen or heard before. The words felt familiar.
to bring something back from memory. She could not recall the formula.
to know something when you see it again.
something that seems true but is not. An illusion of knowing.
a series of steps that repeat.

source: The testing effect was shown by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke (2006) and many others. Lena is invented for this lesson.

method.x: Whatever you are studying, the cycle is the same. The tools change with the material.

items.x: Say each thing in your own words. If you cannot, you are not ready to memorise.
Give each item a vivid picture (room 2): a keyword, a character, a scene.
Put the pictures on pegs, in a palace or in a chain.
Close the notes. Write or say everything you can. Check, and mark what you missed.
Test again tomorrow, then in three days, then in a week.

method.title: A one-hour session
method.given: Forty minutes of new material, twenty of testing.
lines: Understand: read the notes once, put each item in your own words.
Picture and place: build the scenes for words, verbs, steps and formulas.
Test yourself: close the notes, write everything, then check.
Fix: re-do the pictures for what you missed. Plan tomorrow's test.
method.pic: Twenty of the sixty minutes are spent with the notes closed. That is where the learning happens.

items: Mix the kinds. Switching between words, verbs and formulas in one session is harder, and helps more than doing one kind at a time.
Ask what you missed. The mistakes are the useful part: fix those pictures.
Stop when you can do it twice. Then leave it, and come back later.

method.x: Explain in one minute why re-reading notes is a weak way to study, and what you will do instead.

try.title: Material and tool
try.prompt: Match each kind of material to the tool.

try.title: Plan your next study session
try.prompt: Choose something you need to learn. Write a one-hour plan with the five steps (understand, picture, place, test, come back) and name the tool you will use for each kind of material.
try.model: Material: 20 French words and 5 irregular verbs. 0 to 10: say each in my own words. 10 to 35: keyword scenes for the words; one story for each verb family. 35 to 55: close the notes, write everything. 55 to 60: fix the misses. Test again tomorrow morning and in three days.
checks: All five steps are in the plan.
At least a third of the time is spent testing.
I know which tool I will use for each kind of material.

try.title: Four scenes at once
try.prompt: Make one short scene each for: the keyword scene for pato (duck), the verb family -ought, the alphabet peg Charlie holding a stamp, and the formula F = ma.
try.model: Pato: a duck in a cooking pot. -ought: a fisherman who bought, brought, caught. Charlie: Chaplin's cane stamps a letter with a giant stamp. F = ma: a fist hits a mouse and it flies like an arrow.
checks: Each of the four has its own scene.
The scenes are different from each other.

items.s: Reading your notes again gives a feeling of ___, but not recall.
The best way to study is to ___ yourself with the notes closed.
After testing, you should ___ again tomorrow.

try.q: Which study session is likely to be the most effective?
opts: Twenty minutes of notes, then twenty minutes testing yourself with the notes closed
try.why: Testing yourself trains recall, which is what the exam asks for.

try.title: Test yourself aloud
try.prompt: Without looking, say the three forms of three irregular verbs, three code words, two Latin roots and one formula.

cards: Recognise: it feels familiar when you see it. Recall: you bring it out with nothing in front of you.
Understand, picture, place, test yourself, come back.
Keyword method: sound-alike + a picture joined to the meaning.
Split it into prefix + Latin root.
Learn the family; one story per family.
Alphabet pegs, one step per peg.
Meaning first, then a character per symbol.

quiz.q: Why does re-reading give a false feeling of knowing?
opts: The material is in front of you, so everything feels familiar

quiz.q: In a one-hour session, how long should you spend with the notes closed?
What should you do with the items you missed?
opts: Fix their pictures and test again
quiz.why: The mistakes show which pictures are weak.

quiz.q: Why mix different kinds of material in one session?
opts: Switching is harder, and strengthens recall
quiz.why: Mixing makes you choose the right tool each time.

challenge.title: Memory challenge: mixed review
challenge.intro: Eight things from the last five rooms, in a mixed order: a foreign word, a root, a verb form, a code word and formulas. Type them back in any order.
challenge.study: Eight scenes: a duck in a pot, a clown throwing a pie, a fisherman who caught, a swimmer who swum, Charlie's cane, an eagle on a cheetah, a fist and a mouse, a tractor pulling.

look_back.q: What does F = ma say in words?
How many code words are there, and what is the first?

look_back.a: Verbs like sing, sang, sung where the vowel goes i, a, u.
Find a sound-alike in your own language and make a picture joining it to the meaning.

can_do: explain why testing myself beats re-reading.
use the five-step cycle for any new material.
choose the right tool for words, verbs, steps and formulas.
reflect: What will you test yourself on this week? When will you test yourself again?
